item_title: The long end sold off to a nineteen-year high while oil sat still, which argues the move was about debt supply rather than the Gulf.
mechanism: The cross-asset divergence is the whole signal. A geopolitical supply shock raises breakevens AND crude together; a fiscal/supply repricing raises long nominal yields while leaving crude alone. Today gave the second pattern cleanly: 30-year to 5.31% and a nineteen-year high, 2-year easing to ~4.17% — a bear steepener — while Brent gave up its early gains despite the US–Iran framework formally expiring on the same day. If the Iran expiry were driving the bond move, the energy complex would be the first place it showed, and it is the one place it did not. That points at term premium — issuance into a debt stock near $40T, and inflation persistence — rather than at the Gulf.

scenarios.direction: The steepening continues and starts to bite on exactly the buildout this map tracks, since AI datacenter financing is long-duration and priced off the long end rather than off the policy rate the Fed-odds debate concerns.
scenarios.why: Twenty-year lease guarantees and multi-decade power contracts discount at the long end; a persistent rise there raises the hurdle rate for projects whose cash flows begin in 2028, which is precisely when the PORTS-Pike leases attach.
scenarios.precedent: The 2022–23 long-end selloff repriced US commercial real estate development economics within two quarters even as short rates plateaued, stalling projects that penciled at lower term premium — the same duration sensitivity, a different asset class.

scenarios.direction: Alternatively this is a one-session auction-and-supply artifact that mean-reverts within the week, and the 19-year-high framing proves to be a round-number headline rather than a regime change.
scenarios.why: A 3bp move from the session open is small in absolute terms, and "highest since" thresholds are crossed and uncrossed routinely without a change in the underlying trend.
scenarios.precedent: The 30-year printed a "highest since 2007" headline on both 2026-05-19 and 2026-07-29 by this map's own record, and on neither occasion did it mark a durable break.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime reading is currently fed by the news sweep and carries Friday's soft retail-sales/consumer-sentiment prints as the live signal, which is a short-end story. This is a long-end story pointing the other way, and the two belong in the same reading rather than in separate ones — flagging it for the next /week refresh, since /daily does not write that file.

item_title: Micron crossed $1,000 a share intraday, completing the move the morning pass could only see in premarket.
mechanism: Sustained memory-price strength is the transmission channel by which the AI buildout shows up in consumer and industrial goods costs — DRAM and HBM tightness driven by AI datacenter demand raises the bill of materials for everything from handsets to vehicles. That makes this rally a leading indicator for a specific inflation impulse working directly against the cooling narrative that just pushed September Fed-hike odds down to ~30%. Today's session added the causal detail the morning pass lacked: sell-side attribution to memory demand broadening from GPU to CPU and outstripping supply through 2027, which is a demand-mix claim rather than a momentum claim, and it sits alongside a long-end selloff in the same session.

scenarios.direction: Memory contract prices keep climbing into September and hand the Fed's hike-leaning minority a concrete goods-inflation data point that cuts against the retail-sales and consumer-sentiment softness currently driving the 30% reading.
scenarios.why: Memory is an input to a wide enough range of finished goods that sustained contract-price increases pass through with a lag, arriving in CPI well after the equity market has priced them.
scenarios.precedent: The 2021 semiconductor shortage passed through into electronics and used-vehicle CPI with a two-to-three quarter lag, and did so while consumer-demand indicators were themselves softening — the same divergence being set up here.

scenarios.direction: ❌ RETIRED ON THE EVIDENCE. The morning pass's alternative — that this was a positioning artifact with no fresh driver, momentum on 08-13/08-14 news — no longer fits: named sell-side analysts put a specific supply/demand thesis behind today's move, and the stock crossed a level rather than drifting toward it. Replaced by a narrower doubt: the pass-through may still fail even if the demand thesis is right, since contract pricing and spot equity enthusiasm have decoupled before.
scenarios.why: A correct read on physical tightness does not guarantee CPI pass-through when downstream manufacturers absorb input costs in margin rather than price, which is the common case in competitive handset and PC markets.
scenarios.precedent: Memory contract prices rose through 2017–18 without a distinguishable electronics-CPI signature, as OEMs absorbed the increase rather than passing it to consumers.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's fund_flows entry already flagged AI-driven inflation pressure on tech goods and electricity from EPFR's 08-11 Global Navigator commentary, but had not connected it to a specific equity move. This connects the two, and sets it against both the rate-cooling reading and today's opposing long-end move.

item_title: Iran claimed a Hormuz transit-route "understanding" with Oman as the 60-day US-brokered window expired; Oman has not confirmed and oil barely moved.
mechanism: Brent's failure to move on the claim is the informative part, and the afternoon strengthened it: crude gave up its early gains and finished the US session near $89–90 even after the framework formally expired and Trump publicly threatened to bomb Oman. With a Hormuz risk premium estimated around 10% already embedded, neither the de-escalation claim nor the escalation rhetoric moved the price — which means the market is discounting BOTH, and pricing a frozen stalemate rather than a directional break. The discount is rationally grounded: the Oman claim is one-sided (Oman silent), Iran conceded the map and joint statement are unfinished, and this map's own 08-16 shipping data showed transits already at zero.

scenarios.direction: Oman confirms independently within the week, and Brent gives back a meaningful part of the embedded premium in a single session because so much of it is priced.
scenarios.why: The premium is large relative to the physical supply at stake, so confirmation from the counterparty that has stayed silent is the specific missing input rather than an incremental one.
scenarios.precedent: The 08-12 US-brokered Iran-Oman announcement produced exactly this shape — a sharp move on the initial claim that partially unwound within days once the terms proved narrower than the headline, and the market has since demanded confirmation before repricing.

scenarios.direction: Oman stays silent past a few more days and the claim decays into noise, leaving the premium intact and the ledger entry unresolved into its 08-19 due date.
scenarios.why: Silence from the party whose waters and ports the arrangement depends on is itself information, and this thread has now logged several Iranian claims of progress that no counterparty corroborated.
scenarios.precedent: Iran's earlier "agreed in principle" characterisation of the Oman talks, logged on this thread, was never matched by an Omani statement and did not produce a durable repricing.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's conflict_risk_premium reading already records iran-oman-hormuz-deal-signing as pending rather than hit. A full session of two-sided headlines with a flat tape is stronger evidence for that pending framing than the morning's flat tape alone.

item_title: NVIDIA's 8-K caps the Ohio guarantee at $105 billion and reveals it is a residual-value guarantee, not a project backstop — with OpenAI indemnifying NVIDIA for every dollar NVIDIA pays.
mechanism: A residual-value guarantee is a fundamentally different instrument from the project backstop the press coverage implied, and the difference cuts both ways. It is NARROWER than feared: NVIDIA does not owe $105B on an OpenAI default, it owes the shortfall between a guaranteed minimum lease value and whatever the site fetches on re-lease or sale — and Pike County datacenter shells with 4.25 GW of interconnect are unlikely to be worthless in any world where AI demand exists at all. But it is also more CORRELATED than a standalone credit exposure, because the scenario that triggers it is the same scenario that destroys the collateral's value: OpenAI's insolvency is not independent of AI datacenter resale prices. The guarantee is worth most when it costs least and least when it costs most. The OpenAI indemnity compounds precisely this: NVIDIA's recourse runs back to the party whose insolvency is the trigger, so the indemnity is worth nearest to nothing exactly when it is called.

scenarios.direction: Analysts and rating agencies converge on a much smaller "economic" exposure than $105B once the residual-value structure is understood, and the headline number stops being quoted as NVIDIA's risk within a few weeks.
scenarios.why: The cap is a gross notional on a shortfall obligation that only attaches from 2028 and amortises against recoverable asset value; credit analysts price such structures off expected loss, not notional, and will say so publicly once they model it.
scenarios.precedent: Aircraft residual-value guarantees written by manufacturers are disclosed at gross maximum exposure but consistently carried by rating agencies at a small fraction of notional — Boeing's and Embraer's RVG books have been treated this way for two decades, with realised losses far below disclosed caps.

scenarios.direction: Alternatively the correlation argument wins: an AI capex downturn severe enough to impair OpenAI simultaneously craters specialised datacenter resale values, the indemnity proves uncollectible, and realised exposure lands far closer to the cap than any expected-loss model predicted.
scenarios.why: Purpose-built AI datacenter shells have a thin buyer set that is itself concentrated in the same handful of firms exposed to the same demand shock, so recovery assumptions drawn from general-purpose real estate or aviation do not transfer.
scenarios.precedent: Merchant power plants built for a single offtaker in the early 2000s were repeatedly resold at 10–30 cents on the dollar precisely because the counterparty's failure and the asset class's glut were the same event — the correlation failure this structure shares.

context_note: This is the single largest quantified entry in the circular-financing picture capital-context.yaml tracks, and the first where the map has contract-level terms rather than reported figures. It should anchor the next /week refresh of that file's AI-financing reading, with the caveat that gross notional and economic exposure are different numbers and only the first is now known.

item_title: Groq raised $350M at $3.5B — half its peak — as a company that now buys Nvidia chips instead of building rivals to them, with Nvidia in the round.
mechanism: This is the vendor-financing thread's stake ladder producing a legible price for the first time. The sequence is unusually clean: Nvidia paid $20B in December for a licensing deal that took Groq's founder and senior silicon team; Groq, hollowed out, abandoned its own LPU architecture; and it now buys and operates the incumbent's chips as a neocloud, funded in part by the incumbent. An independent-silicon competitor was converted into a demand-side customer, and the conversion is visible as a halving of enterprise value from $6.9B to $3.5B. The mechanism worth naming is that acqui-licensing achieves what an acquisition could not: the same competitive result — a rival's roadmap ends — without a merger filing, because no company changed hands and no market share formally moved.

scenarios.direction: The structure attracts antitrust attention as a template rather than as this deal, with regulators or legislators naming acqui-licensing as a merger-review gap in the AI hardware stack.
scenarios.why: The competitive effect is indistinguishable from an acquisition while the transaction form sidesteps the reporting thresholds that would trigger review, and that gap is the kind of structural argument enforcement bodies act on rather than a fact-specific complaint.
scenarios.precedent: The 2024–25 wave of AI acqui-hires — Inflection into Microsoft, Adept and Covariant into Amazon, Character.AI into Google — drew exactly this scrutiny, with the FTC and CMA both opening inquiries into whether the structures evaded merger control, and the CMA formally reviewing the Microsoft/Inflection arrangement.

scenarios.direction: Alternatively it stays commercially unremarkable — a failed chip startup recapitalised by its largest supplier — and the only durable signal is what it says about independent AI-silicon economics, which is that they did not work at $6.9B.
scenarios.why: Groq is small enough that no market-structure conclusion is forced, and the down round can be read as an ordinary correction to a 2025 valuation rather than as evidence about the transaction form.
scenarios.precedent: Graphcore's sale to SoftBank in 2024 at a fraction of its $2.8B peak drew no structural scrutiny at all and was absorbed as an ordinary distressed outcome in AI silicon.

context_note: The thread's stake ladder — Nebius 9.3%, Naver $1B, Intel $5B, Groq ~$20B licensing — has until now been a list of positions with no outcomes attached. This is the first rung with a realised result, and the result is that the counterparty stopped competing. That is worth carrying into how the other three rungs are read.

item_title: Nvidia, OpenAI and SoftBank signed the Ohio guarantee, and the signed terms correct two numbers this map was carrying.
mechanism: The signed structure makes explicit what the vendor-financing thread has only inferred: NVIDIA is now simultaneously the compute supplier, a credit backstop for the site's land/power/shell buildout, and an equity holder in the developer — three positions in one transaction, with OpenAI as the demand side. That concentration is the actual mechanism, not the headline size. ✅ The pricing gap this entry was written around CLOSED the same day, and closed the way its first scenario said it would. Written at 10:00 ET, this interpretation argued that the release named capacity and NVIDIA's $1.5B equity cheque but attached no dollar figure to the guarantee, so the contingent liability could not be aggregated against the rest of the ecosystem's backstops. By 15:00 ET the figure was found — not in later press reporting but in the 8-K filed alongside that very release, at $105B, under Item 2.03. The mechanism reading stands; the illegibility premise does not, and is marked resolved rather than quietly edited away.

scenarios.direction: ✅ RESOLVED SAME DAY. The dollar figure surfaces in NVIDIA's securities disclosure rather than in press reporting, and arrives materially different from the "<$120B" attributed to the deal.
scenarios.why: Securities disclosure obligations bite on quantified contingent liabilities in a way that a press release does not, and the gap between a reported number and a filed one is where this map has already been corrected once this week (the $3B SB Energy figure that turned out to be $1.5B).
scenarios.precedent: NVIDIA's own 13F on 08-14 put filed numbers on SpaceX and Intel stakes that had circulated only as estimates beforehand, and the filed figures differed materially from the estimates — the same report-then-file correction pattern, three days earlier.

scenarios.direction: ❌ RETIRED. That the guarantee is never given a single headline number because it is structured as phase-gated commitments rather than one facility.
scenarios.why: The 8-K does give a single cumulative cap ($105B) for the initial commitment, while separately treating the additional ~3.8 GW as discretionary. So the instrument is BOTH quantified and tranched — the either/or this scenario assumed was a false choice.
scenarios.precedent: Vendor residual-value guarantee programs in aircraft and industrial-equipment leasing are routinely disclosed as aggregate maximum exposure across tranches — which is, in the event, exactly the form NVIDIA used, and it is a quantified form.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's standing picture carries the AI-financing loop as its central open risk, and the 08-15 digest led with bond traders pricing ~$70B of off-balance-sheet backstops. A single $105B capped guarantee is larger than that entire estimated stock — which is the number that now needs carrying forward into the next refresh.

item_title: The 30-year Treasury extended its 19-year high to 5.32% and semis broke together.
mechanism: A rising discount rate is repricing the longest-duration equity in the index; the AI complex's cash flows sit past 2028, which is exactly where a 5.32% 30-year does the most damage.

scenarios.direction: The repricing reaches credit next — AI-exposed spreads widen and the marginal datacenter financing prices worse or not at all.
scenarios.why: Equity duration reprices first because holders can sell instantly, while lenders sit on existing paper; credit follows with a lag of weeks if the rate move proves durable.
scenarios.precedent: This map already logged the leading indicator: investors pulled ~36% of initial orders on US investment-grade issuance in the week to 08-17, twice the prior week's rate — a credit market discriminating before it closes. The 2022 rate shock ran the same sequence, de-rating long-duration tech equity months before issuance windows shut.

scenarios.direction: It stays a multiple event and never reaches financing; semis recover once the long end stabilises.
scenarios.why: The buildout's largest obligations are contracted, not market-funded — NVIDIA's $105B guarantee, Meta's ~$420B, Microsoft's $678B RPO — and contracted capital does not reprice with the tape.
scenarios.precedent: Micron crossed $1,000 on Monday and gave it back Tuesday with no change to the memory shortage underneath it — a multiple moving while the fundamental did not, inside this map's own week.

context_note: Held at plausible, not higher: this is one intraday read at 10:09 ET, and the strong evidence is the co-movement of three names on no news.

item_title: At the close, memory/storage had widened further than the megacaps, the major indexes finished mixed, and a same-day Journal analysis put a bigger number on the accounting-boundary question this map opened Monday.
mechanism: Off-balance-sheet AI commitments sit outside covenant tests and rating triggers, so a widening gap between disclosed debt and real obligations can grow for a long time with no market signal until a stress event forces consolidation onto the balance sheet.

scenarios.direction: A rating agency or auditor forces one hyperscaler to consolidate a material chunk of its off-balance-sheet AI commitments, and the resulting balance-sheet debt jump reprices its credit spread sharply in a single event.
scenarios.why: Lease and take-or-pay structures are consolidated under GAAP/IFRS when the accounting substance overrides the form, and auditors have already flagged at least one such structure as a critical audit matter this year.
scenarios.precedent: EY's February critical-audit-matter flag on Meta's Beignet structure, already on this map, is the live example of an auditor treating an off-balance-sheet AI structure as a genuine judgment call rather than a settled classification.

scenarios.direction: The gap stays a disclosure curiosity — every firm's obligations are contracted against real, growing AI revenue, so no consolidation event or repricing ever triggers.
scenarios.why: Off-balance-sheet treatment under operating-lease and take-or-pay accounting is common and legal for real, performing contracts, and most of the named obligations are tied to currently-profitable AI businesses rather than speculative ones.
scenarios.precedent: Airlines and shipping firms have carried large off-balance-sheet operating-lease books for decades without a systemic consolidation event, because the underlying assets kept earning.

context_note: capital-context.yaml does not yet carry an off-balance-sheet-obligations reading at all; this and the $1.65T Meta-driven figure logged 08-17 are the two data points that should seed one at the next refresh.

item_title: ByteDance drew more than $30 billion of orders for a jumbo bank loan
mechanism: Credit demand for AI-adjacent borrowers is becoming selective rather than disappearing: lenders are repricing risk, not retreating from it.

scenarios.direction: The bifurcation widens — cash-generative borrowers keep clearing big books while SPV- and lease-financed buildout paper pays up.
scenarios.why: An order book tracks the borrower's own cash generation more than the sector's narrative, and the buildout's marginal financing sits a step removed from any operating company's cash flow.

scenarios.direction: It is an idiosyncratic Asian syndicated-loan print with no read across to US issuance at all.
scenarios.why: Asian bank-loan and US public investment-grade order books follow different conventions, so the two figures may simply not be comparable quantities.

context_note: Kept speculative because the comparison spans two markets whose order-book conventions differ; the direction is suggestive, not evidence.

item_title: Xiaomi's profit fell on a worsening memory-chip crunch hitting smartphone demand
mechanism: Datacenter memory demand is bidding DRAM away from consumer devices, so the shortage now taxes a buyer's margin instead of only lifting a seller's multiple.

scenarios.direction: The tax spreads through consumer electronics — more handset, PC and console makers report memory-driven margin compression.
scenarios.why: Memory is a substitute-free commodity input on short contract cycles, so a datacenter-driven price shock reaches every downstream buyer at roughly the same time.
scenarios.precedent: The 2017-18 DRAM shortage ran exactly this path: server demand bid prices up, handset makers absorbed it in margin for two to three quarters, then passed it to retail prices.

scenarios.direction: It stays Xiaomi-specific, a thinner-margin buyer feeling a shock better-hedged rivals have already contracted around.
scenarios.why: Long-term supply agreements and vertical integration insulate the largest handset makers; Samsung makes its own memory and Apple contracts years ahead.
scenarios.precedent: Samsung's dual role as memory supplier and device maker has repeatedly let it net out shortage cycles that hurt pure buyers.

context_note: If the first scenario holds, Memory Squeeze needs a demand-side strand — the story becomes who pays for scarcity, not who profits.

item_title: Anthropic is negotiating a pre-IPO revolving credit facility set to exceed $10 billion — more than four times the $2.5B five-year facility it closed a year ago.
mechanism: A credit facility sized partly by bank competition for IPO underwriting mandates is a weaker signal of balance-sheet need than one sized purely against projected cash burn, so its size should not be read as Anthropic's own liquidity forecast without discounting for that motive.

scenarios.direction: The facility prices and draws are read by analysts as a genuine pre-IPO liquidity cushion, and its size becomes a data point in valuation discussions ahead of the listing.
scenarios.why: A revolver this large, even if partly relationship-driven, still appears on Anthropic's cap table and roadshow materials, where it will be read at face value by investors who were not party to the underwriting-mandate competition behind its size.

scenarios.direction: The facility is downsized before close once the IPO-mandate jockeying settles, landing well under the reported $10B+ figure.
scenarios.why: Reported deal sizes early in syndication routinely shrink once banks that will not win a mandate lose the incentive to over-commit, and this map's own reporting already flags the figure as unsettled.

context_note: Sits next to the $65B run-rate this map logged 08-17 — a company posting that revenue lining up a facility four times its prior size is worth tracking against how much of the increase survives to the actual close.

item_title: Japan's bond market spiked toward its highest yield since 1996 and took the country's AI-proxy stocks down with it — the same rate-into-AI-equities mechanism this map has tracked domestically all week, now visible overseas.
mechanism: A domestic fiscal-policy shock (Japan's FY2027 budget uncertainty) is transmitting into global AI-equity valuations through the same discount- rate channel this map has tracked in US Treasuries all week, showing the mechanism is about duration and rates generally, not a US-specific story.

scenarios.direction: The channel becomes explicitly cross-border — a JGB, Bund or gilt yield spike starts moving US AI-complex names the way US Treasury yields already do, and currency-hedged AI-capex funding costs become a named risk factor analysts track globally.
scenarios.why: AI capex is financed and built by multinational firms (SoftBank, Arm, Japanese chip-equipment makers) whose funding costs and investor bases span borders, so a rate shock anywhere in that chain has no structural reason to stay contained to one currency.
scenarios.precedent: This map's own week: the identical co-movement (equities breaking together with no company-specific news) appeared first in US Treasuries on 08-18 and reproduced in Japan on 08-19 with a named sell-side mechanism, one trading day apart — the fastest repeat of a pattern this map has logged.

scenarios.direction: It stays two separate, locally-caused selloffs that merely rhyme — Japan's move is really about the Takaichi budget and BOJ hike speculation, not an imported US rate story, and the co-movement is coincidence rather than transmission.
scenarios.why: Japan's 10-year yield move is explicitly tied in coverage to domestic fiscal and central-bank triggers distinct from anything in US Treasury markets, so attributing it to the same global channel risks over-reading a shared asset class (AI-proxy equities) as shared causation.

context_note: capital-context.yaml's rate_regime reading is entirely US-Fed-framed; this is the first genuinely cross-border rate/AI-equity data point this map has logged and should seed a non-US leg of that reading at the next refresh.

item_title: The US Treasury doubled its long-bond buyback size and the whole bear-steepener this map has tracked since Monday reversed in a single announcement.
mechanism: A direct liquidity intervention in the long end can reverse a supply-driven yield spike faster than the underlying supply/demand imbalance actually changes, which means today's yield relief is a policy response to a symptom, not evidence the debt-issuance pressure itself eased.

scenarios.direction: The relief holds and buybacks become a recurring tool Treasury leans on whenever long-end yields threaten AI-capex financing costs, effectively capping how far this map's own bear-steepener story can run before policy intervenes again.
scenarios.why: An "at least $4B" cap gives Treasury room to escalate further if needed, and having used the tool once with visible market effect lowers the threshold for using it again.
scenarios.precedent: The 08-13 30-year auction cleared at the highest yield since 2001 with no policy response; six days later the same pressure produced this intervention — the gap between "market absorbs it" and "Treasury acts" narrowed within this map's own week.

scenarios.direction: The relief is temporary and yields resume climbing within days, because the buyback addresses market functioning, not the underlying fiscal deficit and AI-linked issuance volume driving the supply.
scenarios.why: Buybacks retire existing long-dated debt but do not reduce net new issuance, so the structural imbalance this map has tracked all week (record global issuance, a ~36% initial-order pull rate) remains unaddressed by the mechanism used today.

context_note: Directly closes the "what to watch next" note this map logged in the ai-buildout-debt-risk thread on 08-18 — the market-test the thread was waiting on arrived as a policy intervention instead, worth carrying into the next capital-context.yaml refresh as a new named tool in the rate_regime reading.

item_title: SoftBank's own 13F shows the identical mark-only-growth pattern this map found in NVIDIA's 13F a week ago, this time on Intel.
mechanism: When two of the largest disclosed stakeholders in the same distressed asset (Intel) both show mark-only growth with no new buying across the same quarter, it signals conviction is not increasing even as the headline dollar figures suggest deepening commitment — the position sizes are inflating on price, not on demand from their largest holders.

scenarios.direction: More large holders of AI-adjacent turnaround bets (Intel and similar names) show the same pattern in coming 13Fs — mark-only growth, no incremental buying — and analysts start reading 13F dollar totals net of price appreciation before citing them as conviction signals.
scenarios.why: Once the pattern is visible in two of the largest disclosed holders of the same stock within one filing cycle, it becomes a checkable claim rather than a one-off, and analysts who were burned reading NVIDIA's Intel growth as active buying have reason to check share counts before repeating the mistake with SoftBank.
scenarios.precedent: This map's own 08-17/08-18 finding: NVIDIA's Intel position grew $7.93B to $29.99B with an identical share count across both quarters — the same mark-only pattern, filed six days before SoftBank's.

scenarios.direction: The pattern is coincidental rather than a signal about Intel specifically — both NVIDIA and SoftBank simply have not had a trading window to add or trim since their initial strategic investments closed, and the next filing cycle shows active rebalancing from one or both.
scenarios.why: Both stakes originated as strategic, deal-linked investments (NVIDIA's $5B, SoftBank's $2B) rather than open-market accumulation, so a lack of subsequent share-count change may reflect lock-up or strategic-hold terms rather than a market read on Intel.

context_note: Intel fell 26.6% between the 06-30 filing date and 08-14, so both filed marks are already stale in the opposite direction — worth flagging alongside this pattern rather than letting the $12.14B/$29.99B figures stand as current.

item_title: Google took a warrant on up to $12.2 billion of Marvell stock — roughly 7% of the company — structured to vest against future custom- chip revenue rather than paid as equity upfront.
mechanism: A revenue-vesting warrant aligns Google's payoff with Marvell actually delivering custom-chip volume rather than with a fixed equity check, so it functions as a demand guarantee priced in optionality instead of cash — a financing structure genre distinct from the vendor-financing loans and lease guarantees this map has tracked elsewhere in the buildout.

scenarios.direction: The structure becomes a template other hyperscalers use with their own custom-silicon partners (Amazon/Annapurna, Microsoft/Maia), substituting revenue-vesting warrants for the credit guarantees and equity stakes this map has logged from Nvidia and others.
scenarios.why: A warrant that only pays off if the revenue materializes solves the same demand-guarantee problem Nvidia's guarantees and equity stakes address, while costing the hyperscaler nothing upfront if the chip program underdelivers — a strictly better risk profile for the buyer than a cash investment.
scenarios.precedent: This map's own ladder of hyperscaler-to-vendor financing structures (NVIDIA's cash equity stakes, its $105B lease guarantee, GIC/ Macquarie's Theseus equity) has diversified in structure with each new deal logged this month; a warrant is a genuinely new form on that ladder.

scenarios.direction: It stays specific to Marvell/Google's own commercial relationship and is read as a one-off incentive alignment rather than a new financing genre, because Marvell's stock reaction (a sharp pop) is itself evidence the market read it as a vote of confidence rather than a structural innovation worth replicating.
scenarios.why: Warrant structures tied to commercial contracts are a known, long-standing tool in supplier relationships generally, and this deal's prominence may owe more to its size and Marvell's relative smallness than to novelty in the instrument itself.

context_note: chip-hyperscaler-rotation's own watch question — monetization-proven vs. monetization-unproven as the axis that matters, not hyperscaler-vs-chipmaker — gets a new data point: Google structured its bet to pay only on proven monetization, which is itself a read on which side of that axis it expects Marvell's custom-chip revenue to land.

item_title: OpenAI's revenue is reported up 35% this quarter with enterprise revenue up more than 50%, and Ramp card data puts its API spend growth at 82% quarter-on-quarter in Q3 against Anthropic's 76%
mechanism: Circular AI financing is collateralised by forward revenue, so a shift in which lab is growing fastest reprices the loop's counterparties rather than the loop's size.

scenarios.direction: Vendor-financing terms start tracking quarterly revenue share between the two labs, rather than being fixed at deal signing.
scenarios.why: Nvidia, Microsoft and Oracle each hold exposure to specific labs; if relative growth flips twice a year, the natural response is shorter commitment tenors and revenue-linked covenants.
scenarios.precedent: Nvidia halved the Ohio guarantee under investor pressure on 2026-08-15 — already on this map's own timeline, and evidence these commitments are revisable rather than fixed.

scenarios.direction: Nothing reprices, because both labs' growth stays high enough in absolute terms that relative position is noise to lenders.
scenarios.why: 82% and 76% quarter-on-quarter are both extraordinary; a counterparty underwriting either is underwriting the category, not the league table within it.

context_note: Ramp card data is a spend proxy, not a filed figure, and this map has no audited revenue number for either lab this quarter.

item_title: Treasury's long-bond buyback bump has fully round-tripped, and Bessent says he is acting on information the bond market does not have.
mechanism: A buyback changes which maturity investors must hold without changing net Treasury supply, so it can only work as a signal — and a signal the market can test costs credibility when it fails.

scenarios.direction: Treasury escalates on size rather than concede the tool is weak, taking buybacks past Bessent's own $4bn-per-issue floor.
scenarios.why: He has already framed $4bn as a floor and claimed private information the market lacks; both are positions that are harder to retreat from than to double down on.
scenarios.precedent: The 1999-2000 Treasury buyback programme under Rubin and Summers is the closest structural precedent, but it ran against fiscal surpluses rather than deficits — the opposite setup.

scenarios.direction: Issuance composition shifts shorter instead, moving the problem off the long end and onto rollover frequency.
scenarios.why: Shortening duration is the cheaper lever and does not require defending a purchase programme that visibly failed to hold yields down within two sessions.

context_note: Yield levels here are aggregator snapshots rather than primary ticks, and this map still has no thread carrying the long-end story.

item_title: Gold and bitcoin are trading the Treasury intervention as a debasement signal rather than a rates signal.
mechanism: If buybacks read as debt monetisation, the absorbing counterparty is the currency itself rather than any institution, so capital rotates into assets with no issuer standing behind them.

scenarios.direction: The dollar keeps sliding as buyback size scales, and gold and bitcoin go on tracking Treasury announcements rather than yields.
scenarios.why: That is the falsifiable form of the debasement reading — it predicts the dollar, not the curve, is the variable that moves on the next announcement.
scenarios.precedent: The 2020-21 gold and crypto move on Fed balance-sheet expansion is the same trade, though driven by a central bank rather than by the Treasury's own buying.

scenarios.direction: The move fades as a one-week positioning story once buyback auctions clear without incident.
scenarios.why: A buyback creates no new money, and the market may simply be mispricing the difference between Treasury purchases and central-bank purchases for a few sessions.

context_note: Both moves are one-day and one-week readings; nothing here establishes a sustained regime change in the dollar.

item_title: Nvidia took a minority equity stake in Cloverleaf Infrastructure
mechanism: A chip vendor is buying equity in the physical bottleneck that gates its own demand, converting a supply constraint on customers into an asset on its own balance sheet.

scenarios.direction: The pattern keeps moving upstream — power agreements, queue positions and land options become Nvidia-held assets rather than customer problems.
scenarios.why: Power and siting are now the binding constraint on GPU deployment, so the marginal dollar of demand creation is worth more spent there than on customer equity.
scenarios.precedent: Nvidia's existing customer-base stakes — Nebius 9.3%, Intel $5B, Naver $1B, Groq ~$20B licensing — are the same instrument applied one layer downstream, and are already on this thread.

scenarios.direction: It stays a one-off partnership: a few hundred million to secure priority access at named sites, never scaled into a portfolio.
scenarios.why: Owning land-and-power developers carries permitting, community and utility-regulatory exposure that a fabless chip designer has no apparatus to manage at scale.

context_note: No figure is disclosed in the joint release, so the "several hundred million" size rests on outside coverage rather than a filing.

item_title: Broadcom is assembling $70-80bn of debt through a special-purpose vehicle to build AI chip capacity for Anthropic.
mechanism: Compute capacity is being financed off balance sheet through an SPV, so first loss sits with junior lenders rather than with Broadcom or the lab whose demand underwrites the whole structure.

scenarios.direction: The junior tranche prices wide enough that the structure becomes the market's first public estimate of AI-buildout credit risk.
scenarios.why: A junior piece near $35bn is too large to place quietly, so its spread becomes a visible number where none has previously existed for AI lab compute.
scenarios.precedent: The $35bn Broadcom/Apollo/Blackstone partnership announced in June is the same structure at half the size, and is already on this thread's timeline.

scenarios.direction: The raise is cut or restructured before pricing, given reported totals still span $60bn to $100bn across outlets.
scenarios.why: That spread suggests the deal is still being shopped rather than sized, which makes lender appetite the binding constraint rather than Broadcom's stated need.

context_note: Every figure here is sourced to unnamed lenders through press reporting; no filing or signed commitment exists yet.
